entries.h: 🔍 Decoder — find the step in the stem

entries.h: 🚨 The traps that cost you the most points

entries.t: The single most common miss. If the stem ends in indicates, suggests, or the nurse interprets, the answer is a name for the problem, not a thing you do.

entries.h: Picking the intervention you would do second
entries.t: On a "first" question, several options are things you genuinely would do. Assess before you intervene — unless the client is unstable, in which case act first. Never pick "notify the provider" if there is something you m

On "which client first," the sick-looking-but-expected client is bait. A day-two temperature of 100.2 F is expected. A new, unexpected, or worsening finding wins — especially airway, breathing, or circulation.
"Which statement indicates the client needs FURTHER teaching" means you are hunting for the wrong statement. Read the last six words of every stem twice.
On "generate solutions," anything starting with "The nurse will…" is almost always wrong. A goal describes what the client will do, by when.

entries.t: 1. The formula for "how much do I give?" (Desired ÷ Have) × Quantity = amount to give Desired = what the order says. Have = the strength on the label. Quantity = the volume or tablets that strength comes in. ORDER LABEL

entries.h: The formula for "how much do I give?"
entries.t: (Desired ÷ Have) × Quantity = amount to give Desired = what the order says. Have = the strength on the label. Quantity = the volume or tablets that strength comes in. ORDER LABEL SAYS SET-UP ANSWER metoprolol 50 mg 25 mg

The formula only works when Desired and Have are in the same unit. If the order says grams and the bottle says milligrams, fix that first. This is where most wrong answers come from. Order: 0.5 g. Label: 250 mg tablets.
Half a tablet, 2 tablets, 5–15 mL of a liquid: reasonable. 38 tablets or 0.006 mL: you slipped a decimal. On a test, an answer that is off by exactly 1000 almost always means a mg/mcg mix-up.

entries.t: ✅ Answer Raise the head of the bed, suction available, side-lying — anything that keeps feed from going down the throat. (Bonus content, not on Exam 4.)

entries.t: Big picture: Two dials dominate this exam's nutrition — protein (the renal "flip") and fat (the hepatobiliary lever). Nail those two and most questions fall into place. 🫘 Renal & Urinary Nutrition (Module 9) Urea is the
Diet therapy for Renal/Urinary & Hepatobiliary disorders · ATI Nutrition Ch. 14–15
Urea is the waste product of protein metabolism. It rises as kidneys fail, so protein is the master dial — but which way you turn it depends on dialysis.

RESTRICT protein 0.8–1.0 g/kg/day, high biologic value (eggs, meat, fish, soy, dairy). Restrict sodium (for BP) and potassium (prevent hyperkalemia). Restrict phosphorus — limit peanut butter, beans, bran, cola, chocolat

On dialysis, protein INCREASES to 1.0–1.2 g/kg (amino acids are lost in the dialysate). Still low sodium (2–3 g), low potassium, low phosphorus (700–1,200 mg), fluid-restricted, ~35 kcal/kg, phosphate binders with meals.
Usually reversible. 20–30 cal/kg. Protein 0.6 g/kg (no dialysis) → 1.0–1.2 (on dialysis). Fluid = urine output + 500 mL when oliguric.
Proteinuria + edema. Adequate protein 0.7–1.0 g/kg (soy helps), LOW sodium (2,000 mg), carbs for calories, low cholesterol/fat, vitamins.
Mostly calcium oxalate. #1 = FLUIDS for ≥2 L urine/day (including before bed). Limit animal protein, sodium, and oxalates (spinach, rhubarb, beets, nuts, chocolate, tea). No megadose vitamin C.

↑ Protein (positive nitrogen balance) · carbs NOT restricted · vitamins B, C, K · eliminate alcohol, nicotine, caffeine. (In hepatic encephalopathy, protein is temporarily moderated — but the default liver-diet answer is
LIMIT fat — dietary fat stimulates the inflamed gallbladder. Low-fat is the whole answer.
Acute: NPO + NG suction, TPN to rest the pancreas. Chronic: low-fat, high-protein, high-carb + vitamins C & B.

🛡️ acetylcysteine Give within 8–10 hr for best effect. Watch the rising AST/ALT, not the symptoms — the client can look fine while the liver is failing.
🛡️ naloxone Shorter half-life than most opioids — it can wear off and the client re-sedates. Keep monitoring.
🛡️ flumazenil Can trigger seizures in chronic users or mixed TCA overdose. Use cautiously.
🛡️ vitamin K (phytonadione) Add FFP or PCC when bleeding is active — vitamin K alone is too slow.
🛡️ protamine sulfate 1 mg protamine per ~100 units heparin. Monitor aPTT.
🛡️ protamine sulfate (partial) Only reverses about 60% — LMWH is not fully reversible.
🛡️ idarucizumab (Praxbind) Direct thrombin inhibitor with its own dedicated antidote.
🛡️ andexanet alfa Factor Xa inhibitors. Expensive, not stocked everywhere.
🛡️ digoxin immune Fab (DigiFab) Anorexia, nausea, yellow-green halos. Hypokalemia worsens toxicity.
🛡️ calcium gluconate Classic in OB. First sign is loss of deep tendon reflexes, then respiratory depression.
🛡️ deferoxamine Urine turns a reddish 'vin rosé' color as iron is chelated out.
🛡️ succimer, edetate calcium disodium Chelation. Find the exposure source before discharge.
🛡️ atropine + pralidoxime SLUDGE — salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, GI upset, emesis.
🛡️ hydroxocobalamin Suspect after enclosed-space smoke inhalation. Turns urine and skin red.
🛡️ 100% oxygen (hyperbaric if severe) Pulse ox reads falsely normal — draw a carboxyhemoglobin level.
🛡️ leucovorin (folinic acid) 'Leucovorin rescue.' Hydrate and alkalinize the urine.
🛡️ fomepizole (or ethanol) Blocks alcohol dehydrogenase so the toxic metabolite never forms.
🛡️ glucagon Glucagon bypasses the blocked beta receptor. Atropine first for bradycardia.
🛡️ IV calcium + glucagon + high-dose insulin Verapamil and diltiazem drop both rate and pressure.
🛡️ sodium bicarbonate Watch for a widening QRS — that is the sign to treat, not the level.
🛡️ sugammadex, or neostigmine + glycopyrrolate Sugammadex encapsulates rocuronium and vecuronium.
🛡️ physostigmine 'Mad as a hatter, red as a beet, dry as a bone, hot as a hare, blind as a bat.'
🛡️ dextrose 50%, glucagon Conscious and able to swallow? 15 g fast carbs, recheck in 15 min.
🛡️ dantrolene Malignant hyperthermia. Earliest sign is rising end-tidal CO2, not fever.
🛡️ phentolamine Stop the infusion, leave the catheter in to aspirate, then infiltrate the site.
🛡️ aminocaproic acid Stop the infusion first. Have blood products ready.
🛡️ calcium gluconate first Calcium protects the heart, it does not lower the potassium.
🛡️ pyridoxine (vitamin B6) Also given routinely with INH to prevent peripheral neuropathy.
🛡️ calcium gluconate Tingling around the mouth, tremors, prolonged QT. See the Blood Products page.
🛡️ epinephrine Then antihistamines, steroids, oxygen and fluids.

entries.h: 🚨 The rules that apply to every transfusion

entries.h: ⭐ Any reaction — the order of actions
entries.t: 1. STOP the transfusion → 2. NS with NEW tubing → 3. Vitals + assess → 4. Notify provider + blood bank → 5. Send bag, tubing & samples New tubing matters — if you keep the old line open you keep infusing the product.

entries.h: 🚨 Three rules that keep you out of trouble
entries.t: Only normal saline goes with blood. No LR in liver failure or hyperkalemia. It contains potassium and needs the liver to convert lactate. Correct sodium slowly — no more than about 8-10 mEq/L in 24 hours.

entries.h: 🚨 Ask about supplements in every medication reconciliation

entries.h: ⏰ When to Take It — and Why
entries.t: Timing rules are not arbitrary. Each one exists because something goes wrong without it. Learn the reason and you will not have to memorize the list. 🚨 The four that hurt people Bisphosphonates — full glass of water, upr

Bisphosphonates — full glass of water, upright 30 minutes. Lying down burns the esophagus. Extended-release — never crush. Crushing an ER opioid delivers a whole day at once. Steroids and beta blockers — never stop abrup

entries.h: ⭐ Empty stomach or with food? The one-line version
entries.t: Empty stomach = food would block absorption. With food = the drug would tear up the stomach, or food helps it absorb. Before meals = it has to be in place before the food arrives.

entries.h: 🚨 The traps that cost you the most points

entries.t: The single most common miss. If the stem ends in indicates, suggests, or the nurse interprets, the answer is a name for the problem, not a thing you do.

entries.h: Picking the intervention you would do second
entries.t: On a "first" question, several options are things you genuinely would do. Assess before you intervene — unless the client is unstable, in which case act first. Never pick "notify the provider" if there is something you m

On "which client first," the sick-looking-but-expected client is bait. A day-two temperature of 100.2 F is expected. A new, unexpected, or worsening finding wins — especially airway, breathing, or circulation.
"Which statement indicates the client needs FURTHER teaching" means you are hunting for the wrong statement. Read the last six words of every stem twice.
On "generate solutions," anything starting with "The nurse will…" is almost always wrong. A goal describes what the client will do, by when.

entries.h: 🔍 Decoder — find the step in the stem
entries.t: The verb in the question tells you the step. Learn these phrases and the step names itself. IF THE STEM SAYS… STEP THEN ANSWER… "Which finding should the nurse report?" · "Which findings are consistent with…?" Recognize

entries.h: 🚨 The traps that cost you the most points

entries.t: The single most common miss. If the stem ends in indicates, suggests, or the nurse interprets, the answer is a name for the problem, not a thing you do.

entries.h: Picking the intervention you would do second
entries.t: On a "first" question, several options are things you genuinely would do. Assess before you intervene — unless the client is unstable, in which case act first. Never pick "notify the provider" if there is something you m

On "which client first," the sick-looking-but-expected client is bait. A day-two temperature of 100.2 F is expected. A new, unexpected, or worsening finding wins — especially airway, breathing, or circulation.
"Which statement indicates the client needs FURTHER teaching" means you are hunting for the wrong statement. Read the last six words of every stem twice.
On "generate solutions," anything starting with "The nurse will…" is almost always wrong. A goal describes what the client will do, by when.

entries.t: Answer: Hildegard Peplau Peplau published Interpersonal Relations in Nursing (1952) and described the phases and roles of the nurse–client relationship.

entries.t: Answer: Philippe Pinel (or William Tuke) Pinel (France) and Tuke (England) championed the concept of asylum as a humane refuge in the 1790s.

entries.h: Identify the drug classification for: Clozapine (Clozaril)
entries.t: Answer: Atypical (second-generation) antipsychotic Clozapine is the prototype atypical antipsychotic; requires weekly WBC monitoring due to risk of agranulocytosis.

entries.h: Identify the drug classification for: Fluoxetine (Prozac)
entries.t: Answer: SSRI antidepressant Fluoxetine was the first SSRI approved; first-line treatment for depression and anxiety disorders.

entries.h: Identify the drug classification for: Amitriptyline (Elavil)
entries.t: Answer: Tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) A TCA with strong anticholinergic effects; used for depression and chronic pain; give at bedtime; limit to 7-day supply in suicidal patients.

entries.h: Identify the drug classification for: Benztropine (Cogentin)
entries.t: Answer: Anticholinergic (antiparkinsonian agent) Used to treat EPS (acute dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism) caused by first-generation antipsychotics.

entries.h: Identify the drug classification for: Methylphenidate (Ritalin)
entries.t: Answer: CNS stimulant (for ADHD) Do not take after 4 PM; monitor height and weight in children; habit-forming.

entries.h: Identify the drug classification for: Carbamazepine (Tegretol)
entries.t: Answer: Anticonvulsant used as a mood stabilizer Risk of blood dyscrasias; monitor CBC. Also used for bipolar disorder and trigeminal neuralgia.

entries.h: Identify the drug classification for: Clonazepam (Klonopin)
entries.t: Answer: Benzodiazepine Anti-anxiety agent; ends in "-pam"; risk of dependency; do not stop abruptly; contraindicated in pregnancy.

entries.h: Identify the drug classification for: Quetiapine (Seroquel)
entries.t: Answer: Atypical (second-generation) antipsychotic Ends in "-pine"; treats both positive and negative symptoms of schizophrenia; metabolic syndrome risk.
